newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan merges business income tax at 25 pct.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan merges business income tax at 25 pct.

text.p: Taiwan's Finance Ministry announced on Wednesday it would merge the island's two income taxes into one business income tax and set the merged rate at 25 percent.
Finance Minister Paul Chiu said it would recoup a sharp downturn in state revenues arising from the reform by assessing a 10 percent levy on profits that enterprises reserve rather than reinvest.
"The new tax system will avoid double taxation and will help corporate structures," Chiu said at a morning news conference.

Word of the 25 percent merged tax rate was leaked last week but ministry officials did not settle on how to make up for the shortfall the reform would create until a closed-door meeting early on Wednesday.
Other proposals to close the gap, which were put forward by a blue-ribbon tax reform committee, included cutting government spending and increasing Taiwan's value-added tax.
The ministry had considered setting the merged business income tax rate at 35 percent, but junked the idea in early October amid intense opposition from the business community.
Chiu said foreign nationals' taxes were not affected because their maximum assessments already were capped at 25 percent.

Technically speaking, what the ministry has called a "two-into-one" tax merger is actually an accounting change that eliminates double taxation of companies' profits and the dividends they pay to shareholders.
As a result, maximum assessments on individuals' income will be capped at 40 percent, sharply below the maximum 55 percent for which they were liable before the merger.
"In fact this is a tax reduction," Chiu told reporters. "It will encourage investment (in Taiwan) and increase our international competitiveness."

The official announcement that the business income tax rate would be fixed at 25 percent had little effect on the island's stock market, which had spiked upward 1.12 percent on October 3 after the decision was first leaked.
Chiu said the ministry policy would be put to the cabinet and parliament for final approval, and said if all goes well the reforms could take effect in 1998.
Economists, including members of the expert panel, have estimated the tax merger would reduce state tax revenues by about T$26.8 billion (US$975 million) a year.

The proposal to set the business tax rate at 35 percent would have yielded a T$4.6 billion (US$167 million) annual windfall, but was shot down by business groups who complained that Taiwan's high taxes were discouraging investment.

Taiwan has been trying to woo the Asia-Pacific operations centres of major multinationals by boosting local economic competitiveness, but the scheme has been hobbled by the slow pace of promised market liberalisation, including tax reform.
